case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
case.limits: The court read the statute's word individual and expressly left open how much AI assistance a human inventor may use. The unsettled question is inventorship quality, not machine inventorship, which is closed.
case.holding: An inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person, so a patent application naming an AI system as the sole inventor is properly refused without reaching whether the system actually conceived anything.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The controlling answer to AI-invented subject matter: whatever a system devises, the application must name a human inventor. Companies cite it when structuring filings around human contributors; challengers cite it to attack patents where the human contribution looks nominal.

reading.body:
Thaler v. Vidal settled that an AI system cannot be named as an inventor, but left open how much AI assistance a human inventor may use.

The Federal Circuit decided the case on the statutory word "individual," holding that an inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person. It did not reach whether the system in question conceived anything, so the ruling is about who can be named, not about what a machine can do. The court expressly reserved the question of how much AI assistance a human inventor may receive.

That reservation is where the practical risk sits. A patent application must name a human inventor, and the doctrine is cited both by companies structuring filings around human contributors and by challengers attacking patents where the human contribution looks nominal. The dispute has moved from machine inventorship, which is closed, to inventorship quality, which is not.

The data covers one appellate holding, one citation, and one live case citing it, University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC. It does not establish a threshold for sufficient human contribution, and no such threshold appears in the record here. Nothing in this data ties the question to compute, buildings, or power.
